# Valaris Limited (VAL) — Forensic Dossier

*Interrogator note: the supplied transcripts span 2024-Q3 through 2025-Q2 and END BEFORE the single most important corporate event in this name's history — the Feb-9-2026 definitive all-stock merger with Transocean (RIG) at a fixed 15.235 exchange ratio. The transcripts therefore describe a STANDALONE Valaris that no longer exists as an independent investment thesis. Every forward-looking statement in the calls below ("return all FCF to shareholders," "patient fleet management," "book-end the white space") has been overtaken by the decision to sell the company into RIG stock. I flag this throughout; the dossier reads management's standalone credibility, then re-frames it against the deal that the transcripts could not see coming.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across the four-quarter window the core story is remarkably **stable and disciplined**, and that is itself the tell. CEO Anton Dibowitz hammers the same three-part message every call: (1) deliver operational performance (revenue efficiency 96–98% every quarter), (2) execute the commercial strategy — "secure attractive long-term contracts for our high-specification fleet," and (3) "prudently manage our fleet and costs."

The arc that DID evolve is the **demand-timing story**. In 2024-Q3 management openly conceded "a meaningful amount of customer demand being deferred into 2026" — projects "delayed as opposed to being canceled." Through 2024-Q4 and into 2025 the refrain hardened into a forward-loaded thesis: a "robust pipeline of deepwater project approvals in 2026 and 2027… at their highest level in more than a decade." By 2025-Q2 that pipeline began converting: backlog climbed to **$4.7B, "the highest it has been this decade,"** with "$1 billion in new backlog" added each of the last two quarters. The narrative thus arced from *"there's a 2025 air-pocket, trust us on 2026"* to *"the 2026 conversion is now happening."*

The growth driver quietly introduced and then leaned on hard is **fleet high-grading and capital return** — "$100M of shares repurchased in Q3," "we remain committed to returning all future free cash flow to shareholders unless there is a better or more value-accretive use for it" (2024-Q3). That caveat — *"unless there is a better use"* — is, in hindsight, the seed of the merger. The thing that was dropped: any pretense of near-term (2025) drillship utilization; management repeatedly guided utilization to "trough in the first half of 2026."

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim (transcript) | Financial evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Strong, durable up-cycle… backlog highest this decade" (2025-Q2: $4.7B) | Revenue +0.3% YoY; 3-yr CAGR +13.9%. Backlog is real but **revenue is flat** — backlog is forward, not yet earned. | **Mixed** — backlog growth real; current revenue does NOT yet show it. |

The forensic core: management's *operational* claims (revenue efficiency, backlog, safety) are **fully corroborated and credible**. The *financial-quality* claims are weaker than the GAAP headline — the 41.5% net margin and +170% EPS are inflated by fleet-sale gains and a favorable arbitration, not by 31x-justifying cash earnings (TTM FCF $117M against an ~$6.5B equity value pre-deal).

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable-to-rising, consistently measured.** Dibowitz never oversells. Telling exchange (2024-Q3, Kurt Hallead): *"it looks like the stock is trading like the cycle is over"* — Dibowitz responds, *"markets are fickle… we feel good about the strength and duration of the cycle."* He is defending a stock the market hated, calmly, with fundamentals.

- **2024-Q3:** Defensive-tinged — "demand deferred into 2026," warm-stacking DPS-5/DS-10, "willing to be patient."
- **2024-Q4:** More decisive — *retiring* three semis (DPS-3/5/6), "we will not hesitate to remove rigs."
- **2025-Q1:** Offensive — "added more than $1 billion in new contract backlog… since our last call just two months ago."
- **2025-Q2:** Most confident — backlog $4.7B "highest this decade," "3 of 4 near-term drillships contracted," asset sale (VALARIS 247 for $108M cash).

The shift is from *defensive patience* (2024) to *commercial momentum* (2025). No language degradation, no guidance walk-backs. This is a high-integrity management team — which matters because it means the eventual decision to SELL to RIG was not a desperation move; it was a considered "better use of capital" judgment by credible operators.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium-High.** EBITDA guidance was hit or slightly beaten each quarter (Q3'24 $150M "better than guidance"; Q4'24 $142M "slightly below midpoint due to a non-cash legal accrual"; Q1'25 $181M; Q2'25 $201M — a clean ascending sequence). Analysts circled the same wound every call: **the 2025 white space.** Kurt Hallead (2024-Q3): "the stock is trading like the cycle is over." 🔴 **Insiders net sellers** (1 buy / 5 sells, open-market).

The standalone "deep-value, Graham MoS 87%, fair value $178" framing in the screener is **obsolete**: the stock is now mechanically pegged to RIG's share price via the 15.235 ratio, not to Valaris's own intrinsic value.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The single most load-bearing phrase in the entire transcript set is the 2024-Q3 caveat: *"we remain committed to returning all future free cash flow to shareholders **unless there is a better or more value-accretive use for it.**"* Management telegraphed, a year early, that they would consider strategic alternatives over buybacks. The 2025-Q2 mention that the "dual-activity arbitration benefited the second quarter" and has "a right to appeal… high bar" shows them clearing legal overhangs — also consistent with deal prep. The consolidation logic the calls keep circling (need for "scale," "manage your fleet as a portfolio") is precisely the rationale RIG/VAL cite for the merger ($200M+ synergies, 73-rig combined fleet, ~$10B backlog).

# VALARIS (VAL) — Forensic Dossier

*Interrogator: Claude Opus 4.8 · Capital-committee dossier · 8-quarter transcript window 2024-Q3 → 2025-Q3, cross-referenced to the screener financial trajectory and live filings.*

> **Frame-breaking fact the transcripts do NOT contain (verified live, 2026-06-18):** On **February 9, 2026** Transocean (RIG) agreed to acquire Valaris in an **all-stock** deal — a **fixed exchange ratio of 15.235 RIG shares per VAL share**, ~$5.8B equity / ~$17B combined EV, pro-forma ~47% VAL / 53% RIG. The transcripts in this packet (through 2025-Q3) all PREDATE the deal, so every "long-term value creation for *our* shareholders / buyback" statement below is now moot — Valaris is no longer a standalone go-forward equity, it is a stock-for-stock **merger arb** whose value is mechanically RIG × 15.235. On **May 4, 2026** the DOJ issued a **Second Request** (HSR), and Australia's ACCC opened a review (Jun 16, 2026). Read the dossier with that overlay.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across the five calls the story is strikingly *consistent* — almost rehearsed — which is itself the tell. Management (CEO Anton Dibowitz, CFO Chris Weber, CCO Matt Lyne) hammers the same three pillars every quarter: (1) operational excellence (revenue efficiency 95–98%), (2) commercial execution (bookend the "white space," secure long-term contracts for the high-spec 7th-gen drillship fleet), (3) disciplined cost/fleet management (warm-stack idle rigs to ~$60k/day, retire/scrap sub-spec semis, return all FCF via buyback).

The one genuine *evolution* is the demand timeline sliding right. In 2024-Q3 management already conceded "a meaningful amount of customer demand being deferred into 2026" (delayed FPSOs, regulatory approvals, customer capital discipline) — but framed it as "delayed, not cancelled." By 2025-Q1 (post-"Liberation Day" tariffs + OPEC+ unwind) the language hardened to "heightened uncertainty," yet they insisted tenders "largely appear on track." By 2025-Q3 they had successfully "bookended the white space" — all four near-term-available drillships re-contracted (DS-10 West Africa, DS-12 to BP Egypt) — and pivoted to a **more constructive long-term macro** ("structurally tighter market later in the decade," IEA 90%-of-upstream-spend-just-to-offset-declines). Backlog climbed steadily $4.7B (2025-Q2) → $4.9B (2026-Q1).

The quietly-dropped thread: the aggressive **$100M/quarter buyback** of 2024 (H2-2024 returned 100% of FCF) decelerated to **$75M in 2025-Q3** and the buyback was explicitly de-committed ("may not necessarily be linear," 2025-Q2). That deceleration foreshadowed the cash-flow trough — and, in hindsight, a board that had decided the standalone path was worth selling.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Mgmt claim | Quarter | Hard evidence | Verdict |

| Returns justify the multiple | implicit | **ROE −62.7%, ROIC −3.6%** | **False on returns.** The company does **not** earn its cost of capital; "41% net margin" is an artifact of a small post-reorg equity base, not franchise quality |

Peer-comps file independently rules it "in_line, not a mispricing" |

The narrative is materially **richer than the numbers justify** on returns and FCF, and roughly *honest* on backlog and the demand-deferral risk (they told you the trough was coming).

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable-to-mildly-declining**, with a defensive drift.
- 2024-Q3: confident but already defensive — "manage *through* this up-cycle," warm-stack DS-10/DPS-5, "markets are fickle... it looks like the stock is trading like the cycle is over" (Kurt Hallead pushback).
- 2025-Q1: most defensive — tariffs/OPEC+ "heightened uncertainty," repeated "three things within our control" (operations, commercial, cost) — textbook shift from offense to **defense/efficiency** language.
- 2025-Q3: re-offensive on the *long-term* macro ("structurally tighter market later in the decade," IEA decline math) while conceding the *near-term* trough ("utilization will trough late this year or early next... exit '26 ~90%"). Confidence in the asset, hedged on the timing.

Guidance got *less* specific on capital return over time (buyback "not linear") and management increasingly leaned on third-party macro (Rystad <$50 breakeven, IEA) rather than its own bookings — a subtle confidence tell.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY — **Medium-High**

Operationally they deliver: revenue efficiency guided ~96% and hit 95–98% four straight years; "bookend the white space" was *promised* repeatedly and *delivered* (4/4 drillships contracted by 2025-Q3); V-247 sale for $108M announced 2025-Q2 and progressing. The screener shows **beat 4/7 qtrs (57%)** — middling, consistent with a company that hits operational targets but whose *earnings* are whipsawed by reactivation costs, legal accruals, and the cycle. The demand-trough warning (first flagged 2024-Q3) **came true on schedule** in 2026-Q1 — they did not sandbag the bad news, which raises credibility. Reliability: **Medium-High on operations, Medium on financial outcomes** (cycle + capital-intensity make EBITDA/FCF lumpy and hard to forecast).

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **"The stock trades like the cycle is over"** (Hallead, 2024-Q3) — the single most prescient question. Management had no answer beyond "markets are fickle." It was right: the equity de-rated until a buyer stepped in.
- **White-space / gap-fill risk** (Eddie Kim, David Smith, repeatedly) — how long are DS-12/DS-15/DS-18 idle, can you fill the gaps? Management consistently conceded "probably not enough [short-term work] to fill all the rigs."
- **Buyback durability** (Josh Jayne, 2025-Q2) — pushed on whether to keep buying; management hedged to "not linear." That hedge aged into the cash trough.
- **Petrobras cost-down pressure** (Doug Becker, 2025-Q3) — Petrobras "looking across their entire supply chain for savings in 2026"; management deflected to "very early days, constructive." A real margin risk left unquantified.
- **FID pushback at low oil** (Eddie Kim) — "is there a Brent level where FIDs get pushed?" Management: "we have not seen programs pushed." Partly contradicted by their own admission of demand deferrals into 2026.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **ROIC −3.6% / ROE −62.7%** — does not earn cost of capital; the "41% net margin" is a thin-equity mirage.
🔴 **EBITDA cliff to $67M and a net loss in 2026-Q1** — the trough management warned of, now real; FCF negative on reactivation capex.
🔴 **Buyback decelerated then de-committed** ($100M→$75M→"not linear") — the standalone FCF-return thesis weakened *before* the sale.
🔴 **Flat revenue (+0.3%)** under a "robust up-cycle" narrative — the cycle is in the backlog/futures, not the trailing P&L.
🔴 **All-stock sale, no cash, no premium floor** (live overlay) — the board chose to merge rather than keep compounding; insiders are net sellers (open-market: 1 buy 7.5k sh vs 5 sells 110k sh).
🟢 **Backlog $4.9B, highest this decade** — the durable asset; the reason RIG paid.
🟢 **Fleet high-graded** — 12 of 13 drillships are 7th-gen, highest concentration in the industry; 12 floaters retired over 5 yrs (most of any driller).
🟢 **Operational delivery** — 95–98% revenue efficiency, clean safety record, contracts secured ahead of need.
🟢 **Told the truth about the trough** — credibility-positive.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The phrase **"long-term value creation for our shareholders"** appears in literally every call — and in Feb-2026 the board cashed that phrase out as an **all-stock combination**, the surest signal that management/board judged the *standalone* re-rate insufficient versus scale. A serial buyer-of-its-own-stock that stops buying and agrees to be acquired is telling you the private-market value > its own read of public-market upside.
- **Petrobras "supply-chain savings"** + Saudi "rig call-backs" framed as positives, but both are NOC pricing leverage over the contractor — a quiet admission day rates have "troughed in the high-300s/low-to-mid-400s" (2025-Q3 Q&A), i.e. the rate cycle peaked.
- Recurring **"warm-stack / preservation-stack / retire"** vocabulary (DPS-3/5/6 scrapped, 147/148/143 stacked) = a fleet being *shrunk and defended*, not grown — consistent with an industry consolidating, which is exactly what the RIG deal completes.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING (terminally) — from a standalone deep-value cyclical into an all-stock merger-arb.** The single most important thing the director must weigh: **VAL is no longer valued on its parts or its cycle — it is valued at RIG × 15.235 with NO cash floor and a live DOJ Second-Request break risk.** The screener's "$178 fair value / 116% MoS" is a book-value artifact that four of five intrinsic methods (DCF/EPV/OwnerErn/IV15) flatly reject; do not size on it. Any position here is a **bet on (a) the deal closing despite heightened antitrust scrutiny of 2-of-3-major-driller consolidation, and (b) RIG's share price** — not on Valaris's intrinsic value, which on cash returns (ROIC −3.6%) does not clear its cost of capital.

**MOAT:** **NARROW, ERODING.** The only durable edge is scale + a high-spec 7th-gen fleet (a scale-cost advantage in a capital-intensive, consolidating industry) — but offshore drilling is a price-taking, cyclical, commodity-leveraged service with **negative ROIC**, NOC customers exerting cost-down pressure (Petrobras, Saudi), and day rates that have "troughed." High margins on thin equity are not a moat; the franchise does not earn its cost of capital. The cure for the lack of moat was *consolidation* — hence the sale.

**SECULAR THREAT:** **manageable, not terminal.** Energy-transition is the relevant structural lens (energy-transition-loser), but offshore deepwater is the *low-cost, low-carbon-intensity* end of the oil supply stack (<$50 breakeven on ~75% of forward FIDs per Rystad; IEA decline math supports sustained upstream spend). The threat to terminal value is **cyclical day-rate/oil risk and capital intensity**, not imminent demand obsolescence. The cheapness, such as it is, is a **post-bankruptcy book artifact + cyclical-trough fear-print**, not a melting base — but it is also **not idiosyncratic alpha**: it is fully captured (and capped) by the RIG exchange ratio.

bull_thesis:
Valaris owns one of the best offshore drilling fleets in the world and is being bought for a 32% premium by the largest operator in the industry, so the bull case runs on two engines that reinforce each other. The first is the deal. On 9 February 2026 Valaris agreed to be acquired by Transocean; every Valaris share converts into 15.235 Transocean shares. The stock closed at $62.41 on 6 February, the last day before the news, so the terms were struck about 32% above the undisturbed price. Transocean's chief executive told investors on the 6 August 2026 results call that the companies expect to complete in the fourth quarter of this year. The US national-security review cleared on 29 June 2026. At Transocean's price of $5.85 on 4 September, the terms are worth $89.12 a Valaris share against a Valaris price of $86.74 — so a buyer today collects roughly 2.7% if the deal simply closes, and then owns the combined company.

The second engine is what that combined company would be worth. Offshore drilling has spent five years consolidating — Noble bought Diamond, and this deal takes the number of serious deepwater fleets down again — while the underlying demand picture has quietly improved. The International Energy Agency's own arithmetic, cited by management in October 2025, is that nearly 90% of global upstream oil spending is needed simply to offset the natural decline of existing fields. Roughly 70% of the deepwater projects due to be approved over the next three years break even below $50 a barrel; Brent has since run to about $96 following renewed conflict in the Middle East over the weekend of 29-30 August 2026. Day rates for the best rigs held above $400,000 straight through the worst utilisation trough of this cycle, which is the clearest evidence yet that the industry's supply discipline is real.

Valaris itself is coming out of that trough on the timetable management promised. It said in July and October 2025 that drillship use would bottom in the first half of 2026 and recover; the first quarter of 2026 was indeed the low, with revenue of $465m and a small loss, and the second quarter recovered to $539m with earnings of $0.72 a share against a Street estimate of $0.46. Backlog — the revenue already contracted — stands at roughly $4.7bn, the highest of the decade, and Petrobras extended two Brazilian contracts in April 2026. Analysts' consensus has 2027 earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation at about $958m, nearly double 2026's expected $540m, and 2027 earnings of $7.00 a share. Valuing the business by its parts on those 2027 numbers at what the market pays for Noble and Transocean today gets to roughly $105 a share. If the deal closes and the 2027 deepwater tightening arrives, Transocean shares at $7.22 — still below their own 52-week high of $7.66 — would make each Valaris share worth about $110.
bear_thesis:
The bear case starts with a number that is not real. Our screener shows a fair value of $178 and a margin of safety of 105%, both built on reported earnings of $13.86 a share for 2025. That figure is an accounting entry. Valaris earned $552m before tax in 2025 but reported $983m of net income; the gap is a net tax benefit of $427m, and $680m of that landed in a single quarter — the fourth of 2025 — against just $36m of pre-tax profit, when the company wrote a long-dormant deferred tax asset back onto its balance sheet. No cash moved. Taxed normally, 2025 earnings were roughly $6 a share, not $13.86. The same entry inflates book value: of $46.40 of book value per share, $19.40 is that tax asset. Of the five valuation methods run on this name, only the one anchored on reported earnings and book value says cheap; the cash-flow and earnings-power methods all read fully valued. There is no deep-value discount here to capture.

Second, the cash. Free cash flow has been negative for three consecutive quarters — minus $39m, minus $26m and minus $92m — and minus $29m over the last twelve months, because capital spending is running at roughly $100m a quarter, about 2.3 times depreciation, on reactivations and regulatory surveys. Cash fell from $676m in September 2025 to $541m in June 2026. Net debt including leases is $624m. Return on invested capital is about 5.5%, below any sensible cost of capital, five years after a bankruptcy that destroyed $4.5bn of shareholder value. Buybacks, which management once described as a commitment to return all future free cash flow, stopped entirely in 2026.

Third, and most important, a buyer today is not buying Valaris. Because the consideration is Transocean shares at a fixed ratio with no collar and no cash component, there is no floor under the value: if Transocean falls, the Valaris holder falls with it, one for one. And Transocean is the more fragile of the two. It carries about $4.6bn of net debt against Valaris's $624m, into a tape where the Federal Reserve is roughly 58-60% priced to raise rates on 15-16 September and the spread between the weakest and second-weakest corporate credit tiers sits at the 99.9th percentile of its three-year range. Valaris holders are being asked to swap a one-times-leverage balance sheet for a four-to-five-times one at the exact moment the market is repricing leverage. Transocean at $4.60 would make each Valaris share worth $70.

Fourth, the deal can still fail. The Department of Justice issued a second request — a demand for extensive additional documents, the step that precedes any serious antitrust challenge — on 4 May 2026. The parties agreed not to certify compliance before 31 July and cannot close until 60 days after they do. As of today no definitive merger proxy has been filed and no shareholder vote has been scheduled, seven months after announcement. If the deal breaks, the roughly 32% takeout premium goes with it. The undisturbed price was $62.41; adjusted forward for the sector's move since, a break puts the stock near $70, and a break combined with a 2027 that falls short of the near-doubling of profit the consensus assumes would take it toward the low $50s — roughly book value, and close to the $46.70 low of the past year.

Finally, there is a governance tell. Management spent five consecutive earnings calls explaining why the upcycle was durable, and in October 2025 forecast that all ten active drillships would be working by the end of 2026. Fifteen weeks later the board sold the company for paper. Either the standalone case was weaker than described, or scale is the only way to earn a return in this business — and neither reading supports paying up for the shares today.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not about the merger — that is efficiently priced — but about what this company is worth without it, and our own screener is on the wrong side of it.

The screen says Valaris is a deep-value name with a fair value of $178 and a 105% margin of safety, on reported 2025 earnings of $13.86 a share growing 171%. interrogator_dossier:
# Valaris Limited (NYSE: VAL) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared 7 September 2026. Share price used throughout: $86.74 (New York close, US dollars). Transcript record supplied covers five consecutive calls, from the third quarter of 2024 through the third quarter of 2025. The three quarters since then are read from the company's own filings, results releases and dated news, because no later call transcript was available in our data feed. Where that distinction matters, it is stated.*

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Valaris runs offshore drilling rigs — thirteen high-specification drillships that drill in deep water, a fleet of shallow-water jackup rigs, and a half share of ARO Drilling, a joint venture with Saudi Aramco. It sells rig-days at a daily rate. The story management told across the five calls has one spine and one very large ending that the calls themselves never reach.

**The spine (late 2024 through late 2025): "the upcycle is real, we just have to bridge a soft patch."** In October 2024 the chief executive, Anton Dibowitz, opened with conviction: the company "maintains our conviction in the strength and duration of this up cycle" while conceding that "we have seen some customer demand deferred." The soft patch was explained precisely and, to management's credit, consistently: customers were pushing projects into 2026 because of "availability of production equipment, delayed FPSOs, protracted regulatory approvals and customers' capital discipline." The key framing, repeated in every subsequent call, was that "projects are being delayed as opposed to being canceled."

**A tightening of the story into a specific, testable promise (February 2025).** The fourth-quarter 2024 call introduced the phrase that became the company's operating objective for the year: bookending the white space. Four of the high-specification drillships had gaps between contracts; the job was to secure long-term work on the far side of the gap and then, if possible, fill the near side. Management also began retiring rigs rather than defending fleet size, announcing the scrapping of three semisubmersibles including one that had been working as recently as the third quarter of 2024. Over five years they had retired twelve floaters, "more than any other offshore driller."

**Delivery (May through October 2025).** The promise was kept, on schedule and verifiably. In May 2025 they reported more than $1 billion of new backlog in two months. In July 2025 another $1 billion-plus took total backlog to "approximately $4.7 billion, the highest it has been this decade," with drillship day rates "above $400,000." By the October 2025 call, with the award of the DS-12 to BP offshore Egypt, "all 4 of our drillships with near-term availability are now contracted for work beginning next year." The year's stated objective was completed.

**A forward call that also proved right.** In July and October 2025 management put a dated, falsifiable forecast on the record: drillship utilisation would "trough in the first half of 2026," seventh-generation rigs would "exit 2026 with utilization levels around 90%," and, in Mr Dibowitz's words in October 2025, "we expect that all 10 of our active drillships will exit '26 on contract and working." The first half of 2026 did indeed prove to be the low point — revenue bottomed at $465 million in the first quarter of 2026 with a small loss, then recovered to $539 million in the second quarter with earnings of $0.72 a share against a Street estimate of $0.46.

**The ending the transcripts never mention.** On 9 February 2026 — three months after the last call in our record — Valaris agreed to be acquired by Transocean, its larger, more heavily indebted competitor, in an all-stock transaction. Valaris holders are to receive 15.235 Transocean shares for each Valaris share. The stock closed at $62.41 on 6 February, the last trading day before the announcement, and $83.82 on the day itself, a rise of about 34%. On Transocean's price that Friday, the terms represented roughly a 32% premium.

That is the arc: eight quarters of a management team explaining, patiently and in detail, why investors should trust the durability of an upcycle and the quality of its fleet — followed, four months after the most confident of those calls, by the sale of the company for paper.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials

| Management's claim | Where and when | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "We remain committed to returning all future free cash flow to shareholders" | Third quarter 2024 | True while it lasted: $100m of buybacks in the third quarter of 2024, $75m in the third quarter of 2025, $24m in the fourth. Then nothing — zero repurchases in both the first and second quarters of 2026. Free cash flow over the last twelve months is **negative $29 million** | Poorer than the story. The 2026 halt is explained by merger restrictions, but the underlying cash was not there either |
| The upcycle is durable; contracting will convert | Every call | Backlog did grow from roughly $4.0bn to $4.7bn-plus, day rates held above $400,000, and all four idle drillships were contracted. This is the claim that verifies best | Matches |
| Utilisation troughs in the first half of 2026, recovery follows | July and October 2025 | Correct. First quarter 2026 revenue $465m and a loss of $0.24 a share; second quarter recovered to $539m and $0.72, beating estimates | Matches, and on the stated timetable |
| Earnings power is inflecting | Implied by the headline fiscal 2025 result of $13.86 a share, up 171% | **This is where the file breaks.** Fiscal 2025 pre-tax income was $552m. The reported net income was $983m. The difference is a net **tax benefit of $427m**, of which a single **$680m non-cash credit landed in the fourth quarter of 2025 against just $36m of pre-tax profit that quarter** — the release of a valuation allowance against deferred tax assets. Taxed normally, fiscal 2025 earnings were roughly $6 a share, not $13.86 | Far richer than the trajectory justifies |
| Fleet quality and scale drive returns | Every call | Return on invested capital is about 5.5% over the last twelve months and the screener's own read is negative. The company still has not earned its cost of capital since emerging from bankruptcy in 2021, when it wrote off $4.5bn | Poorer than the story |
| Capital discipline | Every call | Capital spending is running at roughly $100m a quarter — **2.3 times depreciation** — on reactivations, upgrades and special surveys. This, not weak trading, is why free cash flow is negative through the trough | Honest but under-emphasised |

Two forensic points deserve to be lifted out of the table.

**The fiscal 2025 earnings figure is an accounting event, not a business event.** A deferred tax asset is a stored-up future tax deduction. When a company decides it will probably be profitable enough to use one, it writes the asset onto the balance sheet and the write-on runs through the income statement as a one-off gain. Valaris did this in the fourth quarter of 2025. No cash moved: the cash-flow statement shows the same $688m as a non-cash deferred-tax line. The balance sheet now carries **$1.345 billion of tax assets**, which is $19.40 of the company's $46.40 book value per share. Any valuation method anchored on reported 2025 earnings per share or on book value is therefore anchored on the same single accounting entry twice over. Our own screener's headline — a fair value of $178 and a margin of safety of 105% — comes from exactly that anchoring, and it is wrong. Of the five valuation methods run on this name, only the book-and-earnings-based Graham method says cheap; the discounted-cash-flow, earnings-power and intrinsic-value methods all read fully valued.

**Free cash flow has been negative for a year.** Quarterly free cash flow ran $128m positive in the third quarter of 2025, then negative $39m, negative $26m and negative $92m. Cash fell from $676m in September 2025 to $541m in June 2026. Net debt, on the company's balance sheet at 30 June 2026, is **$624 million** including capitalised leases (about $546m excluding them). This is a liability, not a cushion.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rising, then abruptly silent.** There is no deterioration in the transcript record — which is precisely what makes the February 2026 sale so striking.

- *Third quarter 2024 — confident but defensive.* The language is about protecting value through a gap: warm stacking rigs, cutting costs to "about $60 a day" from an operating level "of around $150 a day," waiting. When an analyst put it bluntly — "it looks like the stock is trading like the cycle is over" — Mr Dibowitz answered "I agree, markets are fickle."
- *Fourth quarter 2024 — disciplined and specific.* "We are willing to be patient to find the right jobs for our rigs... we will not hesitate to remove rigs from our fleet when it makes economic sense."
- *First quarter 2025 — the most defensive moment.* Tariffs and the unwinding of OPEC production cuts "have introduced new uncertainties." Management leaned on a third-party statistic (Rystad: roughly 70% of deepwater projects to be sanctioned break even below $50 a barrel) rather than on its own bookings.
- *Second quarter 2025 — the tone turns.* "The pipeline of floater opportunities that we have discussed in recent quarters are converting into contracts." Backlog at a decade high. This is the most confident call in the set.
- *Third quarter 2025 — confident and forward-leaning.* "The long-term outlook for our industry is becoming increasingly constructive," supported by an International Energy Agency figure that nearly 90% of global upstream spending is needed merely to offset natural field decline. The chief executive then made his most specific forward commitment: all ten active drillships working by the end of 2026.

The shift over the five calls is from defensive (cost, stacking, patience) to offensive (backlog, conversion, utilisation forecasts) — the opposite of the pattern that usually precedes a sale.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: medium-to-high on operations, low on capital returns.**

What they promised and delivered:
- Bookend the white space on four drillships during 2025 — **delivered**, completed by the October 2025 call.
- Utilisation troughs in the first half of 2026 — **delivered**; the first quarter of 2026 was the low.
- Revenue efficiency (the share of contracted revenue actually earned) of 95–98% every quarter — **delivered** across the whole record.
- Retire uneconomic rigs — **delivered**; three semisubmersibles scrapped, jackup 247 sold for $108m in cash.

Where the record is weaker:
- Returning "all future free cash flow to shareholders" was said when the cash was there and quietly became conditional when it was not. To be fair, the chief financial officer, Chris Weber, did flag in July 2025 that returns "may not be a linear line" — a hedge placed before the cash flow rolled over, which is the honest sequence.
- The quarterly earnings-beat record of five in seven is respectable but is flattered by the same tax noise that distorts the annual figure. Two of the eight quarters in the financial record swing on the tax line alone: a $194m charge in the first quarter of 2025 turned $154m of pre-tax profit into a $38m loss, and the $680m credit in the fourth quarter turned $36m of pre-tax profit into $718m of net income. Investors relying on reported earnings per share to judge this business were reading noise.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Three subjects came up repeatedly and were answered thinly.

**Day rates on the Saudi jackup extensions.** In May 2025, Barclays asked directly whether five-year extensions on five ARO-leased jackups were priced at or below prior levels. The answer was a non-answer with a nudge: "unfortunately we're not able to disclose day rates... What I say is the rates are above the historic rates and I would describe them — some people have done the back calculation based on the backlog and I think those folks are pretty smart." Deflected, then hinted at. Saudi Aramco had suspended 27 jackups in the region the previous year; the pricing of those extensions is material and was never disclosed.

**Petrobras cost reduction.** In October 2025 an analyst asked what Brazil's national oil company — one of Valaris's largest customers and the world's largest floater buyer — was asking for in cost concessions for 2026. The commercial chief, Matt Lyne, confirmed Petrobras was "looking across their entire value supply chain for potential savings" and then said it was "too soon to kind of discuss the specifics." Six months later, in April 2026, Petrobras extended contracts with Valaris and Seadrill — but on terms nobody on that call was told about.

**Capital returns.** Asked in July 2025 whether the buyback would continue given "strong" free cash flow and $900m of liquidity, management pointed to the $108m rig sale as the source of "increased flexibility." Buybacks then stopped altogether after a token $24m in the fourth quarter. The topic analysts pushed hardest on turned out to be the one where the answer changed most.

**And the question nobody asked.** Across five calls, not one analyst asked whether Valaris would consider merging or selling itself. Management volunteered nothing. Four months after the last of these calls, the company agreed to be acquired.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- *Fourth quarter 2025.* Reported earnings of $10.32 a share on $36m of pre-tax income. A tax entry produced 69% of the entire year's reported profit. Any screen that reads reported earnings will misprice this company badly, and ours did.
- *Fourth quarter 2025 through second quarter 2026.* Free cash flow negative in three consecutive quarters, with capital spending at 2.3 times depreciation. The trough was funded from the balance sheet.
- *February 2026.* The sale itself. Selling four months after telling investors the outlook was "increasingly constructive" and that every active drillship would be working by the end of 2026 is a governance signal in its own right. Either the standalone case was less robust than described, or the board judged that scale — the acquirer's, not its own — was the only way to earn a return in this industry. Both readings sit uneasily with the calls.
- *Ongoing.* Insider behaviour is one-sided in the wrong direction: on open-market transactions only, one purchase of 7,500 shares against five sales totalling 110,403 shares. This is a weak signal in a company being acquired for stock, but it is not a supportive one.
- *May 2025 and October 2025.* Two of the three largest customer relationships — Saudi Aramco through ARO, and Petrobras — were discussed with pricing deliberately withheld.

**Green flags**

- *2025, whole year.* The commercial objective set in February was met in full by October: four idle high-specification drillships contracted, backlog to a decade high of $4.7bn, day rates above $400,000.
- *Every quarter in the record.* Revenue efficiency of 95–98% and a first half of 2025 with no lost-time injuries. Operating execution is genuinely strong and is the reason customers keep re-hiring the same rigs.
- *February 2025 onward.* Willingness to scrap rather than defend. Retiring an active rig (DPS-5) rather than warm-stacking it indefinitely, and selling jackup 247 for $108m in cash, is capital discipline of the kind this industry historically lacked.
- *First and second quarters of 2026.* The trough forecast proved right and the second quarter beat by a wide margin ($0.72 against $0.46 expected).

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**A vocabulary that migrates from "we will grow into it" to "we will manage through it."** Early calls are about earnings and cash-flow growth. From February 2025 the recurring phrases are prudent fleet management, tightly controlling costs, and reducing expenses during extended idle periods. Growth language never disappears, but it is increasingly outsourced to third parties — Rystad's breakeven statistics, the International Energy Agency's decline-rate figure, Petrobras's fleet plans. The company's own bookings do the talking only in the middle two calls of the five.

**The scale argument arrives early and is never withdrawn.** In October 2024: "One of the reasons you need scale in this business is to be able to manage your fleet as a portfolio." In July 2025 the same logic supports being able to sit rigs on the sidelines. Read forward from February 2026, this is the intellectual groundwork for the merger — management had been arguing the case for scale for eighteen months before selling to the largest operator in the industry.

**The DS-12 award as the closing act.** Contracting the last uncontracted drillship in October 2025 completed the stated objective and cleaned up the asset for sale. Whether or not that was the intent, a fully contracted fleet with backlog at a decade high is the condition in which a seller gets its best price — and the deal was signed fifteen weeks later at a 32% premium.

**The rig market's own structure changed underneath.** In October 2025 Mr Dibowitz observed that day rates "have troughed as we see it for the cycle in the kind of high 300s, low to mid-400 range." Rates held through the worst utilisation trough of the cycle. That is genuine evidence of supply discipline, and it is the strongest single argument that this industry's economics are structurally better than they were a decade ago.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Classification: PIVOTING.** This is not a company executing a plan; it is a company that executed a plan and then sold itself. Operating performance was strong and the stated commercial objectives were met on time. But the capital-allocation story reversed twice in eighteen months — from returning all free cash flow to shareholders, to funding a negative-cash-flow trough from the balance sheet, to handing the whole enterprise to a competitor for shares.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing.** Valaris is no longer a decision about offshore drilling. It is a decision about whether one owns 15.235 shares of Transocean per share, at a small discount, while a US Department of Justice review runs. The acquirer is more leveraged than the target — roughly $4.6bn of net debt against Valaris's $624m — and the payment is shares, not cash, so there is no floor under the value. Everything about the standalone business is now second-order. Anyone underwriting this name on the screener's fair value of $178 is underwriting an accounting entry from December 2025.

**Economic moat: NARROW.** The moat type is scale-and-asset-quality. It is real: twelve of thirteen drillships are seventh-generation units, the highest concentration in the industry, and management's own figures put seventh-generation day rates roughly 25% above sixth-generation and utilisation nearly ten percentage points higher. Customers demonstrably re-hire the same rigs, and rates held above $400,000 through the utilisation trough — evidence of pricing power that did not exist in the last cycle. But the width is limited by the evidence that matters most: return on invested capital of about 5.5%, below any sensible cost of capital, five years after a bankruptcy that destroyed $4.5bn. A moat you cannot see in the returns is a narrow one. **Trend: STABLE** — day rates held at the trough and the industry is consolidating (this deal, and Noble's earlier purchase of Diamond), which should widen it, but the returns evidence does not yet support calling it widening.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** The obvious candidate is the energy transition, and over a twenty-year horizon it is real. Within the horizon that matters here, the evidence points the other way. Deepwater is among the lowest-cost and lowest-carbon-intensity sources of new supply; roughly 70% of deepwater projects to be sanctioned break even below $50 a barrel against a five-year forward price above $65; the International Energy Agency's own arithmetic says nearly 90% of upstream spending is required simply to offset field decline. Brent has since run to roughly $96 on renewed Middle East conflict. The cheapness in this name is therefore not a melting-terminal-value problem — but nor is it cheapness. The optical discount is a tax artefact, and on the measure that cannot be gamed, enterprise value against 2027 consensus earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, Valaris trades near 6.9 times against roughly 8.1 times for Noble: a modest discount on a forecast that requires the business to nearly double that measure from 2026's level. That is a fair price for a good fleet, not a mispricing.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

bull_thesis:
Valaris owns one of the best offshore drilling fleets in the world and is being bought for a 32% premium by the largest operator in the industry, so the bull case runs on two engines that reinforce each other. The first is the deal. On 9 February 2026 Valaris agreed to be acquired by Transocean; every Valaris share converts into 15.235 Transocean shares. The stock closed at $62.41 on 6 February, the last day before the news, so the terms were struck about 32% above the undisturbed price. Transocean's chief executive told investors on the 6 August 2026 results call that the companies expect to complete in the fourth quarter of this year. The US national-security review cleared on 29 June 2026. interrogator_dossier:
# Valaris Limited (NYSE: VAL) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared 7 September 2026. Share price used throughout: $86.74 (New York close, US dollars). Transcript record supplied covers five consecutive calls, from the third quarter of 2024 through the third quarter of 2025. The three quarters since then are read from the company's own filings, results releases and dated news, because no later call transcript was available in our data feed. Where that distinction matters, it is stated.*

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Valaris runs offshore drilling rigs — thirteen high-specification drillships that drill in deep water, a fleet of shallow-water jackup rigs, and a half share of ARO Drilling, a joint venture with Saudi Aramco. It sells rig-days at a daily rate. The story management told across the five calls has one spine and one very large ending that the calls themselves never reach.

**The spine (late 2024 through late 2025): "the upcycle is real, we just have to bridge a soft patch."** In October 2024 the chief executive, Anton Dibowitz, opened with conviction: the company "maintains our conviction in the strength and duration of this up cycle" while conceding that "we have seen some customer demand deferred." The soft patch was explained precisely and, to management's credit, consistently: customers were pushing projects into 2026 because of "availability of production equipment, delayed FPSOs, protracted regulatory approvals and customers' capital discipline." The key framing, repeated in every subsequent call, was that "projects are being delayed as opposed to being canceled."

**A tightening of the story into a specific, testable promise (February 2025).** The fourth-quarter 2024 call introduced the phrase that became the company's operating objective for the year: bookending the white space. Four of the high-specification drillships had gaps between contracts; the job was to secure long-term work on the far side of the gap and then, if possible, fill the near side. Management also began retiring rigs rather than defending fleet size, announcing the scrapping of three semisubmersibles including one that had been working as recently as the third quarter of 2024. Over five years they had retired twelve floaters, "more than any other offshore driller."

**Delivery (May through October 2025).** The promise was kept, on schedule and verifiably. In May 2025 they reported more than $1 billion of new backlog in two months. In July 2025 another $1 billion-plus took total backlog to "approximately $4.7 billion, the highest it has been this decade," with drillship day rates "above $400,000." By the October 2025 call, with the award of the DS-12 to BP offshore Egypt, "all 4 of our drillships with near-term availability are now contracted for work beginning next year." The year's stated objective was completed.

**A forward call that also proved right.** In July and October 2025 management put a dated, falsifiable forecast on the record: drillship utilisation would "trough in the first half of 2026," seventh-generation rigs would "exit 2026 with utilization levels around 90%," and, in Mr Dibowitz's words in October 2025, "we expect that all 10 of our active drillships will exit '26 on contract and working." The first half of 2026 did indeed prove to be the low point — revenue bottomed at $465 million in the first quarter of 2026 with a small loss, then recovered to $539 million in the second quarter with earnings of $0.72 a share against a Street estimate of $0.46.

**The ending the transcripts never mention.** On 9 February 2026 — three months after the last call in our record — Valaris agreed to be acquired by Transocean, its larger, more heavily indebted competitor, in an all-stock transaction. Valaris holders are to receive 15.235 Transocean shares for each Valaris share. The stock closed at $62.41 on 6 February, the last trading day before the announcement, and $83.82 on the day itself, a rise of about 34%. On Transocean's price that Friday, the terms represented roughly a 32% premium.

That is the arc: eight quarters of a management team explaining, patiently and in detail, why investors should trust the durability of an upcycle and the quality of its fleet — followed, four months after the most confident of those calls, by the sale of the company for paper.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials

| Management's claim | Where and when | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "We remain committed to returning all future free cash flow to shareholders" | Third quarter 2024 | True while it lasted: $100m of buybacks in the third quarter of 2024, $75m in the third quarter of 2025, $24m in the fourth. Then nothing — zero repurchases in both the first and second quarters of 2026. Free cash flow over the last twelve months is **negative $29 million** | Poorer than the story. The 2026 halt is explained by merger restrictions, but the underlying cash was not there either |
| The upcycle is durable; contracting will convert | Every call | Backlog did grow from roughly $4.0bn to $4.7bn-plus, day rates held above $400,000, and all four idle drillships were contracted. This is the claim that verifies best | Matches |
| Utilisation troughs in the first half of 2026, recovery follows | July and October 2025 | Correct. First quarter 2026 revenue $465m and a loss of $0.24 a share; second quarter recovered to $539m and $0.72, beating estimates | Matches, and on the stated timetable |
| Earnings power is inflecting | Implied by the headline fiscal 2025 result of $13.86 a share, up 171% | **This is where the file breaks.** Fiscal 2025 pre-tax income was $552m. The reported net income was $983m. The difference is a net **tax benefit of $427m**, of which a single **$680m non-cash credit landed in the fourth quarter of 2025 against just $36m of pre-tax profit that quarter** — the release of a valuation allowance against deferred tax assets. Taxed normally, fiscal 2025 earnings were roughly $6 a share, not $13.86 | Far richer than the trajectory justifies |
| Fleet quality and scale drive returns | Every call | Return on invested capital is about 5.5% over the last twelve months and the screener's own read is negative. The company still has not earned its cost of capital since emerging from bankruptcy in 2021, when it wrote off $4.5bn | Poorer than the story |
| Capital discipline | Every call | Capital spending is running at roughly $100m a quarter — **2.3 times depreciation** — on reactivations, upgrades and special surveys. This, not weak trading, is why free cash flow is negative through the trough | Honest but under-emphasised |

Two forensic points deserve to be lifted out of the table.

**The fiscal 2025 earnings figure is an accounting event, not a business event.** A deferred tax asset is a stored-up future tax deduction. When a company decides it will probably be profitable enough to use one, it writes the asset onto the balance sheet and the write-on runs through the income statement as a one-off gain. Valaris did this in the fourth quarter of 2025. No cash moved: the cash-flow statement shows the same $688m as a non-cash deferred-tax line. The balance sheet now carries **$1.345 billion of tax assets**, which is $19.40 of the company's $46.40 book value per share. Any valuation method anchored on reported 2025 earnings per share or on book value is therefore anchored on the same single accounting entry twice over. Our own screener's headline — a fair value of $178 and a margin of safety of 105% — comes from exactly that anchoring, and it is wrong. Of the five valuation methods run on this name, only the book-and-earnings-based Graham method says cheap; the discounted-cash-flow, earnings-power and intrinsic-value methods all read fully valued.

**Free cash flow has been negative for a year.** Quarterly free cash flow ran $128m positive in the third quarter of 2025, then negative $39m, negative $26m and negative $92m. Cash fell from $676m in September 2025 to $541m in June 2026. Net debt, on the company's balance sheet at 30 June 2026, is **$624 million** including capitalised leases (about $546m excluding them). This is a liability, not a cushion.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rising, then abruptly silent.** There is no deterioration in the transcript record — which is precisely what makes the February 2026 sale so striking.

- *Third quarter 2024 — confident but defensive.* The language is about protecting value through a gap: warm stacking rigs, cutting costs to "about $60 a day" from an operating level "of around $150 a day," waiting. When an analyst put it bluntly — "it looks like the stock is trading like the cycle is over" — Mr Dibowitz answered "I agree, markets are fickle."
- *Fourth quarter 2024 — disciplined and specific.* "We are willing to be patient to find the right jobs for our rigs... we will not hesitate to remove rigs from our fleet when it makes economic sense."
- *First quarter 2025 — the most defensive moment.* Tariffs and the unwinding of OPEC production cuts "have introduced new uncertainties." Management leaned on a third-party statistic (Rystad: roughly 70% of deepwater projects to be sanctioned break even below $50 a barrel) rather than on its own bookings.
- *Second quarter 2025 — the tone turns.* "The pipeline of floater opportunities that we have discussed in recent quarters are converting into contracts." Backlog at a decade high. This is the most confident call in the set.
- *Third quarter 2025 — confident and forward-leaning.* "The long-term outlook for our industry is becoming increasingly constructive," supported by an International Energy Agency figure that nearly 90% of global upstream spending is needed merely to offset natural field decline. The chief executive then made his most specific forward commitment: all ten active drillships working by the end of 2026.

The shift over the five calls is from defensive (cost, stacking, patience) to offensive (backlog, conversion, utilisation forecasts) — the opposite of the pattern that usually precedes a sale.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: medium-to-high on operations, low on capital returns.**

What they promised and delivered:
- Bookend the white space on four drillships during 2025 — **delivered**, completed by the October 2025 call.
- Utilisation troughs in the first half of 2026 — **delivered**; the first quarter of 2026 was the low.
- Revenue efficiency (the share of contracted revenue actually earned) of 95–98% every quarter — **delivered** across the whole record.
- Retire uneconomic rigs — **delivered**; three semisubmersibles scrapped, jackup 247 sold for $108m in cash.

Where the record is weaker:
- Returning "all future free cash flow to shareholders" was said when the cash was there and quietly became conditional when it was not. To be fair, the chief financial officer, Chris Weber, did flag in July 2025 that returns "may not be a linear line" — a hedge placed before the cash flow rolled over, which is the honest sequence.
- The quarterly earnings-beat record of five in seven is respectable but is flattered by the same tax noise that distorts the annual figure. Two of the eight quarters in the financial record swing on the tax line alone: a $194m charge in the first quarter of 2025 turned $154m of pre-tax profit into a $38m loss, and the $680m credit in the fourth quarter turned $36m of pre-tax profit into $718m of net income. Investors relying on reported earnings per share to judge this business were reading noise.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Three subjects came up repeatedly and were answered thinly.

**Day rates on the Saudi jackup extensions.** In May 2025, Barclays asked directly whether five-year extensions on five ARO-leased jackups were priced at or below prior levels. The answer was a non-answer with a nudge: "unfortunately we're not able to disclose day rates... What I say is the rates are above the historic rates and I would describe them — some people have done the back calculation based on the backlog and I think those folks are pretty smart." Deflected, then hinted at. Saudi Aramco had suspended 27 jackups in the region the previous year; the pricing of those extensions is material and was never disclosed.

**Petrobras cost reduction.** In October 2025 an analyst asked what Brazil's national oil company — one of Valaris's largest customers and the world's largest floater buyer — was asking for in cost concessions for 2026. The commercial chief, Matt Lyne, confirmed Petrobras was "looking across their entire value supply chain for potential savings" and then said it was "too soon to kind of discuss the specifics." Six months later, in April 2026, Petrobras extended contracts with Valaris and Seadrill — but on terms nobody on that call was told about.

**Capital returns.** Asked in July 2025 whether the buyback would continue given "strong" free cash flow and $900m of liquidity, management pointed to the $108m rig sale as the source of "increased flexibility." Buybacks then stopped altogether after a token $24m in the fourth quarter. The topic analysts pushed hardest on turned out to be the one where the answer changed most.

**And the question nobody asked.** Across five calls, not one analyst asked whether Valaris would consider merging or selling itself. Management volunteered nothing. Four months after the last of these calls, the company agreed to be acquired.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- *Fourth quarter 2025.* Reported earnings of $10.32 a share on $36m of pre-tax income. A tax entry produced 69% of the entire year's reported profit. Any screen that reads reported earnings will misprice this company badly, and ours did.
- *Fourth quarter 2025 through second quarter 2026.* Free cash flow negative in three consecutive quarters, with capital spending at 2.3 times depreciation. The trough was funded from the balance sheet.
- *February 2026.* The sale itself. Selling four months after telling investors the outlook was "increasingly constructive" and that every active drillship would be working by the end of 2026 is a governance signal in its own right. Either the standalone case was less robust than described, or the board judged that scale — the acquirer's, not its own — was the only way to earn a return in this industry. Both readings sit uneasily with the calls.
- *Ongoing.* Insider behaviour is one-sided in the wrong direction: on open-market transactions only, one purchase of 7,500 shares against five sales totalling 110,403 shares. This is a weak signal in a company being acquired for stock, but it is not a supportive one.
- *May 2025 and October 2025.* Two of the three largest customer relationships — Saudi Aramco through ARO, and Petrobras — were discussed with pricing deliberately withheld.

**Green flags**

- *2025, whole year.* The commercial objective set in February was met in full by October: four idle high-specification drillships contracted, backlog to a decade high of $4.7bn, day rates above $400,000.
- *Every quarter in the record.* Revenue efficiency of 95–98% and a first half of 2025 with no lost-time injuries. Operating execution is genuinely strong and is the reason customers keep re-hiring the same rigs.
- *February 2025 onward.* Willingness to scrap rather than defend. Retiring an active rig (DPS-5) rather than warm-stacking it indefinitely, and selling jackup 247 for $108m in cash, is capital discipline of the kind this industry historically lacked.
- *First and second quarters of 2026.* The trough forecast proved right and the second quarter beat by a wide margin ($0.72 against $0.46 expected).

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**A vocabulary that migrates from "we will grow into it" to "we will manage through it."** Early calls are about earnings and cash-flow growth. From February 2025 the recurring phrases are prudent fleet management, tightly controlling costs, and reducing expenses during extended idle periods. Growth language never disappears, but it is increasingly outsourced to third parties — Rystad's breakeven statistics, the International Energy Agency's decline-rate figure, Petrobras's fleet plans. The company's own bookings do the talking only in the middle two calls of the five.

**The scale argument arrives early and is never withdrawn.** In October 2024: "One of the reasons you need scale in this business is to be able to manage your fleet as a portfolio." In July 2025 the same logic supports being able to sit rigs on the sidelines. Read forward from February 2026, this is the intellectual groundwork for the merger — management had been arguing the case for scale for eighteen months before selling to the largest operator in the industry.

**The DS-12 award as the closing act.** Contracting the last uncontracted drillship in October 2025 completed the stated objective and cleaned up the asset for sale. Whether or not that was the intent, a fully contracted fleet with backlog at a decade high is the condition in which a seller gets its best price — and the deal was signed fifteen weeks later at a 32% premium.

**The rig market's own structure changed underneath.** In October 2025 Mr Dibowitz observed that day rates "have troughed as we see it for the cycle in the kind of high 300s, low to mid-400 range." Rates held through the worst utilisation trough of the cycle. That is genuine evidence of supply discipline, and it is the strongest single argument that this industry's economics are structurally better than they were a decade ago.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Classification: PIVOTING.** This is not a company executing a plan; it is a company that executed a plan and then sold itself. Operating performance was strong and the stated commercial objectives were met on time. But the capital-allocation story reversed twice in eighteen months — from returning all free cash flow to shareholders, to funding a negative-cash-flow trough from the balance sheet, to handing the whole enterprise to a competitor for shares.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing.** Valaris is no longer a decision about offshore drilling. It is a decision about whether one owns 15.235 shares of Transocean per share, at a small discount, while a US Department of Justice review runs. The acquirer is more leveraged than the target — roughly $4.6bn of net debt against Valaris's $624m — and the payment is shares, not cash, so there is no floor under the value. Everything about the standalone business is now second-order. Anyone underwriting this name on the screener's fair value of $178 is underwriting an accounting entry from December 2025.

**Economic moat: NARROW.** The moat type is scale-and-asset-quality. It is real: twelve of thirteen drillships are seventh-generation units, the highest concentration in the industry, and management's own figures put seventh-generation day rates roughly 25% above sixth-generation and utilisation nearly ten percentage points higher. Customers demonstrably re-hire the same rigs, and rates held above $400,000 through the utilisation trough — evidence of pricing power that did not exist in the last cycle. But the width is limited by the evidence that matters most: return on invested capital of about 5.5%, below any sensible cost of capital, five years after a bankruptcy that destroyed $4.5bn. A moat you cannot see in the returns is a narrow one. **Trend: STABLE** — day rates held at the trough and the industry is consolidating (this deal, and Noble's earlier purchase of Diamond), which should widen it, but the returns evidence does not yet support calling it widening.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** The obvious candidate is the energy transition, and over a twenty-year horizon it is real. Within the horizon that matters here, the evidence points the other way. Deepwater is among the lowest-cost and lowest-carbon-intensity sources of new supply; roughly 70% of deepwater projects to be sanctioned break even below $50 a barrel against a five-year forward price above $65; the International Energy Agency's own arithmetic says nearly 90% of upstream spending is required simply to offset field decline. Brent has since run to roughly $96 on renewed Middle East conflict. The cheapness in this name is therefore not a melting-terminal-value problem — but nor is it cheapness. The optical discount is a tax artefact, and on the measure that cannot be gamed, enterprise value against 2027 consensus earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, Valaris trades near 6.9 times against roughly 8.1 times for Noble: a modest discount on a forecast that requires the business to nearly double that measure from 2026's level. That is a fair price for a good fleet, not a mispricing.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

interrogator_dossier:
# Valaris Limited (NYSE: VAL) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared 7 September 2026. Share price used throughout: $86.74 (New York close, US dollars). Transcript record supplied covers five consecutive calls, from the third quarter of 2024 through the third quarter of 2025. The three quarters since then are read from the company's own filings, results releases and dated news, because no later call transcript was available in our data feed. Where that distinction matters, it is stated.*

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Valaris runs offshore drilling rigs — thirteen high-specification drillships that drill in deep water, a fleet of shallow-water jackup rigs, and a half share of ARO Drilling, a joint venture with Saudi Aramco. It sells rig-days at a daily rate. The story management told across the five calls has one spine and one very large ending that the calls themselves never reach.

**The spine (late 2024 through late 2025): "the upcycle is real, we just have to bridge a soft patch."** In October 2024 the chief executive, Anton Dibowitz, opened with conviction: the company "maintains our conviction in the strength and duration of this up cycle" while conceding that "we have seen some customer demand deferred." The soft patch was explained precisely and, to management's credit, consistently: customers were pushing projects into 2026 because of "availability of production equipment, delayed FPSOs, protracted regulatory approvals and customers' capital discipline." The key framing, repeated in every subsequent call, was that "projects are being delayed as opposed to being canceled."

**A tightening of the story into a specific, testable promise (February 2025).** The fourth-quarter 2024 call introduced the phrase that became the company's operating objective for the year: bookending the white space. Four of the high-specification drillships had gaps between contracts; the job was to secure long-term work on the far side of the gap and then, if possible, fill the near side. Management also began retiring rigs rather than defending fleet size, announcing the scrapping of three semisubmersibles including one that had been working as recently as the third quarter of 2024. Over five years they had retired twelve floaters, "more than any other offshore driller."

**Delivery (May through October 2025).** The promise was kept, on schedule and verifiably. In May 2025 they reported more than $1 billion of new backlog in two months. In July 2025 another $1 billion-plus took total backlog to "approximately $4.7 billion, the highest it has been this decade," with drillship day rates "above $400,000." By the October 2025 call, with the award of the DS-12 to BP offshore Egypt, "all 4 of our drillships with near-term availability are now contracted for work beginning next year." The year's stated objective was completed.

**A forward call that also proved right.** In July and October 2025 management put a dated, falsifiable forecast on the record: drillship utilisation would "trough in the first half of 2026," seventh-generation rigs would "exit 2026 with utilization levels around 90%," and, in Mr Dibowitz's words in October 2025, "we expect that all 10 of our active drillships will exit '26 on contract and working." The first half of 2026 did indeed prove to be the low point — revenue bottomed at $465 million in the first quarter of 2026 with a small loss, then recovered to $539 million in the second quarter with earnings of $0.72 a share against a Street estimate of $0.46.

**The ending the transcripts never mention.** On 9 February 2026 — three months after the last call in our record — Valaris agreed to be acquired by Transocean, its larger, more heavily indebted competitor, in an all-stock transaction. Valaris holders are to receive 15.235 Transocean shares for each Valaris share. The stock closed at $62.41 on 6 February, the last trading day before the announcement, and $83.82 on the day itself, a rise of about 34%. On Transocean's price that Friday, the terms represented roughly a 32% premium.

That is the arc: eight quarters of a management team explaining, patiently and in detail, why investors should trust the durability of an upcycle and the quality of its fleet — followed, four months after the most confident of those calls, by the sale of the company for paper.
